subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 7 of Year 2 Computing at Ehel Academy. That sounds like a very big job, but it just means they ask good questions, collect the answers (which we call data), sort the data into the right kind, and use it to help solve a problem. This unit gives simple names to clever thinking they already do. There are three big ideas, and you build on each other. The first idea is that questions come in two kinds. A statistical question has more than one answer — like “What are the favourite snacks of the children in our class?” A non-statistical question has only one answer — like “What colour is Leo's bag?” The second idea is that the data we collect also comes in two kinds. Numerical data is numbers — things we count or measure, like height or test scores. Categorical data is groups — words like eye colour or favourite fruit. The third idea is the best part: data helps us solve problems. Almost all of this unit is unplugged — it is done on paper, with sorting cards, and with a tape measure. There is no app to download and no account to make. The one place a computer appears is the idea of an electronic form (a set of questions on a screen); you can show what a form looks like on a printed sheet, or on any tablet or phone you already have, but no child ever needs to sign in anywhere.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 2 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Tell a statistical question (more than one answer) from a non-statistical question (only one answer).
Explain, in their own words, that a statistical question is one where the answers can be different for different people.
Name the two kinds of statistical data: numerical (numbers we count or measure) and categorical (groups, like colours or names).
Sort simple data into numerical or categorical.
Understand that we must never add up categorical data — the numbers on a category are just name tags.
Say that computing devices collect data on electronic forms, and that a number is typed or picked, while a category is chosen from a list.
Give at least one way that data helps to solve a problem (test scores, shop stock, weather, or car maps).
Choose the right thing to do with data to answer a question (for example, sort the marks to find the highest).

concepts.title: Questions: one answer or many answers?
concepts.explanation: Questions come in two kinds. A statistical question has more than one answer — the answers can be different for different people. A non-statistical question has only one answer. Being a data scientist starts with knowing which kind of question we are asking. What colour is my bag? Now say: “What is your favourite fruit?” Lots of different answers come back. Some questions have just one answer. Some have many answers.
concepts.example: A many-answer question has a special name — a statistical question. A one-answer question is a non-statistical question.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you tell a one-answer question from a many-answer question?

concepts.title: Two kinds of data: numbers and groups
concepts.explanation: When we ask a many-answer (statistical) question, we collect data. That data comes in two kinds. Numerical data is numbers — things we can count or measure, like height, test scores or how many pets. Categorical data is groups — words that sort things into kinds, like eye colour, favourite fruit or how we travel to school. Some data is numbers we count or measure — that is numerical data. Some data is groups, like colours or names — that is categorical data.
concepts.example: Find one real example of two kinds of data: numbers and groups around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that categorical data is not for adding up, even when it has been given numbers? Can you sort data into numbers (numerical) and groups (categorical)?

concepts.title: Data on a form (computing devices)
concepts.explanation:
Computing devices collect data on electronic forms. A form is just a set of questions. A form can collect both kinds of data: for numerical data you type or pick a number; for categorical data you pick a category from a list (you tap your choice). This is how a phone, tablet or computer gathers data from lots of people quickly.

You can hold up a printed sheet or show one on a tablet you already have.
concepts.example: Find one real example of data on a form (computing devices) around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you tell which questions on the form want a number (numerical) and which want a chosen category (categorical)?

concepts.title: How data helps us solve problems
concepts.explanation:
This is the heart of the unit: data helps us solve problems and decide what to do. Four everyday examples make it real. Teachers look at test scores to see who needs help. Shops keep count of what they sell so you know what to buy more of. Weather computers use rain and wind data to guess tomorrow's weather. Map apps in cars use traffic data to find the quickest way.

A shop at the market writes down what it started with, what it sold, and what is left. Tell the shop story with a simple table.
concepts.example: Answer this in your own words, out loud or on paper: How data helps us solve problems? Then check your answer against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you choose a sensible thing to do with data — sort it, compare it, or add it — to answer a question? Can you give one real way data helps solve a problem?

concepts.title: Be a data scientist: the Mini-Project
concepts.explanation: Working in small groups, they collect real data (each person's height and eye colour), sort each piece of data into numerical or categorical, decide which questions are statistical or non-statistical, and then use the data to answer a question. This session and the Mini-Project go hand in hand. Now you are the data scientist. In your group you will collect two pieces of data about each person — how tall they are, and their eye colour.
concepts.example: Help you measure heights with the tape measure (this is numerical data) and look carefully at eye colour (this is categorical data). Keep groups small — three or four you are plenty.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you use the data to answer a real question, such as who is tallest? Do you collect the data carefully into the table?

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Is "Favourite fruit: mango, banana, dates" numerical or categorical?
Write one way data helps us solve a problem.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Accept any one: a teacher uses test scores to help students; a shop uses sales data to know what to buy; weather computers use rain and wind data to guess the weather; a car map uses traffic data to find the quickest way.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in how data helps us solve problems, and give one example of your own.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
This is the heart of the unit: data helps us solve problems and decide what to do. Four everyday examples make it real. Teachers look at test scores to see who needs help. Shops keep count of what they sell so you know what to buy more of. Weather computers use rain and wind data to guess tomorrow's weather. Map apps in cars use traffic data to find the quickest way.

A shop at the market writes down what it started with, what it sold, and what is left. Tell the shop story with a simple table.

project.title: Unit 7 Project: Be a Data Scientist
project.brief: Bring together everything from Be a Data Scientist into one finished piece of work you can show and explain.
steps: Plan first: write down what your be a data scientist project has to do before you build anything.
Build the smallest version that does one of those things, and run it.
Add one feature at a time, testing after each one.
When something breaks, change one thing, run it again, and note what fixed it.
Check your work against every success criterion below before you call it finished.
successCriteria: I collected my group's height and eye colour in the table.
I said if height is numerical or categorical.
I said if eye colour is numerical or categorical.
I ticked one answer or many answers for each question.
I found the tallest child in my group.

selfAssessment: I can tell a statistical question (more than one answer) from a non-statistical question (only one answer).
I can explain, in their own words, that a statistical question is one where the answers can be different for different people.
I can name the two kinds of statistical data: numerical (numbers we count or measure) and categorical (groups, like colours or names).
I can sort simple data into numerical or categorical.
I can understand that we must never add up categorical data — the numbers on a category are just name tags.
I can say that computing devices collect data on electronic forms, and that a number is typed or picked, while a category is chosen from a list.
I can give at least one way that data helps to solve a problem (test scores, shop stock, weather, or car maps).
I can choose the right thing to do with data to answer a question (for example, sort the marks to find the highest).
